## (a) Definitions

Let $F \colon \mathbf{Ring} \to \mathbf{Sets}$ be a covariant functor (where $\mathbf{Ring}$ denotes the category of commutative rings with $1$).

### 1. Representable

The functor $F$ is called **representable** if there exists a ring $A$ and a natural isomorphism

$$F \;\cong\; \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Ring}}(A,\,-),$$

where $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Ring}}(A,-)$ is the covariant representable functor sending a ring $R$ to the set $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Ring}}(A,R)$ of ring homomorphisms $A \to R$, and acting on morphisms by post-composition. Equivalently (via Yoneda), $F$ is representable if there exists a ring $A$ and a **universal element** $\xi \in F(A)$ such that for every ring $R$, the map

$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Ring}}(A,R) \;\longrightarrow\; F(R), \qquad \varphi \;\longmapsto\; F(\varphi)(\xi)$$

is a bijection, natural in $R$. The pair $(A, \xi)$ is called a **representation** of $F$.

### 2. Zariski sheaf

Recall that the **Zariski topology** on the category of affine schemes (i.e., on $\mathbf{Ring}^{\mathrm{op}}$) has as covering families the localization families: a family of morphisms

$$\{R \to R_{f_i}\}_{i \in I}$$

is a Zariski covering of $\operatorname{Spec} R$ when the elements $f_i \in R$ generate the unit ideal, i.e., $(f_i)_{i \in I} = R$.

The functor $F$ is a **Zariski sheaf** if it satisfies the sheaf condition with respect to every such covering. Concretely: for every ring $R$ and every family $\{f_i\}_{i \in I} \subseteq R$ with $(f_i)_{i\in I} = R$, the diagram

$$F(R) \;\longrightarrow\; \prod_{i \in I} F(R_{f_i}) \;\rightrightarrows\; \prod_{(i,j) \in I \times I} F(R_{f_i f_j})$$

is an **equalizer diagram** (i.e., $F(R)$ is the limit of the right-hand fork). The two parallel arrows are induced by the localization maps:

- the first sends a family $(x_i)_{i}$ to the family whose $(i,j)$-component is the image of $x_i$ under $F(R_{f_i} \to R_{f_i f_j})$;
- the second sends $(x_i)_i$ to the family whose $(i,j)$-component is the image of $x_j$ under $F(R_{f_j} \to R_{f_i f_j})$.

In words: an element of $F(R)$ is uniquely determined by its localizations to all $R_{f_i}$ (locality/gluability), and a compatible family of local sections $(x_i \in F(R_{f_i}))$ — compatible in the sense that $x_i$ and $x_j$ agree after further localization to $R_{f_i f_j}$ — glues uniquely to a global section $x \in F(R)$.

Note that the index set $I$ may be **infinite**, so the products above are arbitrary (set-theoretic) products.

### 3. Open covering of $F$

To define an open covering of $F$ we first need the notion of an **open subfunctor**.

**Open subfunctor.** A subfunctor $U \hookrightarrow F$ (i.e., a monomorphism of functors, given by injections $U(R) \hookrightarrow F(R)$ natural in $R$) is called an **open subfunctor** of $F$ if it satisfies the following condition:

> For every ring $A$ and every element $x \in F(A)$ (equivalently, every morphism $x \colon \operatorname{Spec} A \to F$ from a representable functor), the pullback
> $$U \times_F \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Ring}}(A,-)$$
> is representable by an **open subscheme** of $\operatorname{Spec} A$.

Concretely, this means: for every ring $A$ and every $x \in F(A)$, there exists an ideal $I_x \subseteq A$ (equivalently, an open subset $D(I_x) \subseteq \operatorname{Spec} A$) such that for every ring homomorphism $A \to R$, an element $y \in U(R)$ with $y = F(A \to R)(x)$ exists if and only if $\operatorname{Spec} R \to \operatorname{Spec} A$ factors through the open subset $D(I_x) \subseteq \operatorname{Spec} A$ (i.e., $I_x$ generates the unit ideal in $R$).

**Open covering.** A family $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in \Lambda}$ of open subfunctors of $F$ is called an **open covering** of $F$ if it is **locally surjective** in the following sense:

> For every ring $R$ and every element $x \in F(R)$, the open subsets $(U_\alpha)_x \subseteq \operatorname{Spec} R$ (obtained by pulling back each $U_\alpha$ along $x \colon \operatorname{Spec} R \to F$) **cover** $\operatorname{Spec} R$.

Equivalently: for every $R$ and every $x \in F(R)$, and for every prime ideal $\mathfrak{p} \in \operatorname{Spec} R$, there exists an index $\alpha \in \Lambda$ such that the image of $x$ under $F(R \to R_{\mathfrak{p}})$ lies in $U_\alpha(R_{\mathfrak{p}})$.

The covering is **not required to be finite**: the index set $\Lambda$ may be arbitrary. This is the key point of the parenthetical "(not necessarily finite)" — one allows infinitely many open subfunctors, matching the fact that a Zariski covering $\{D(f_i)\}_{i \in I}$ of $\operatorname{Spec} R$ need not be finite (even though $\operatorname{Spec} R$ is quasi-compact, so any open cover admits a finite subcover, the cover itself need not be finite).

---

**Remark.** The three notions are closely related: if $F$ is representable (say by $A$), then $F \cong \operatorname{Hom}(A,-)$ is automatically a Zariski sheaf (this is the sheaf property of the structure sheaf / the fact that $\operatorname{Spec} A$ is a scheme). The notion of open covering of $F$ generalizes the notion of an open covering of a scheme to arbitrary functors, and the Zariski sheaf condition is precisely the requirement that $F$ satisfies gluing for sections over open coverings of representable functors.
